newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azeri, Japanese firms in Caspian exploration deal.
newsitem.headline: Azeri, Japanese firms in Caspian exploration deal.

text.p: A group of Japanese firms led by Japan National Oil Corporation (JNOC) signed an agreement on Saturday with Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR to explore three offshore Caspian Sea fields.
The Japanese group includes Mitsubishi Oil, IMPEX, and JAPEX. JNOC, acting as a facilitator, will insure risks undertaken by the other three companies in the project.
The memorandum of understanding allows the firms to carry out further exploration on Yanan-Tava, Atashgah and Mugandeniz fields in the south Caspian Sea.
The agreement paves the way for a formal production-sharing deal with SOCAR expected to be signed later this year.
The fields, covering an area of about 500 square kilometres, begin 30 to 40 kilometres offshore. Water depths are 100 to 120 meters.
SOCAR officials said that no information was available on estimated reserves or the eventual size of investment in the project.

"It is simply too early to say anything about the likely reserves or how much money will need to be invested without more sophisticated exploratory work," said SOCAR Vice President for Geology and Geophysics, Khoshbakht Yusif-zade.
But another SOCAR official who did not want to be named described the three fields as "some of our most promising."
Azerbaijan has already signed five contracts with Western oil firms worth more than $15 billion to help develop its massive offshore reserves.
In addition to the Japanese project SOCAR is also in negotiations with American oil giant Exxon to develop three deep-water fields in the South Caspian.
Senior SOCAR officials estimate overall Azeri reserves at about two billion tonnes of crude in addition to seven trillion cubic meters of natural gas.
The biggest contract Azerbaijan has signed to date, worth over $8 billion, is with a 13-member international energy consortium led by British Petroleum and Den norse stats oljeselskap (Statoil).

The Consortium, The Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), must soon announce where it plans to build a new, large pipeline to help carry the bulk of exports from the project, expected to peak after 2005, to Western markets.
Georgia and Russia have been competing for the route but Azeri officials now say the decision has already been made to build the pipeline from Baku to a port on the Georgian Black Sea coast.
Turkey, concerned about tanker traffic through the Bosphorous Straits, says it wants to see the route extended to its Mediterranean coast.
